title: The Neurology of Free Will
coreMove: After a risky loop becomes foreseeable, name the duty to contain, redesign, or avoid its trigger conditions.
sourcePressure: Automatic routines complicate responsibility without erasing it. The source narrows the free-will question into a practical accountability point: explanation matters, but awareness, foreseeability, and deliberate redesign are where duty re-enters.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: The weak version writes a broad free-will essay, excuses all habit-driven behavior, or turns the chapter into simple blame. The writer must keep the focus on knowable loops and the duty to contain or redesign them.

hook: A courtroom speech about free will in the abstract.
A person says they could not help it and the chapter debates philosophy.
A generic confession about a bad habit.
counterintuition: Most people think habits excuse behavior, but actually...
Simple blame solves the accountability problem.
Awareness alone is enough without containment or redesign.
tryThisNow: Set a timer for ninety seconds and forgive yourself.
Write a vague reflection about responsibility.
Promise to be more aware next time.
examples: Generic legal theory without a visible habit loop.
Casino, auction, or shopping loss-control repeats from ch03.
Omniscient surveillance or privacy panic from ch07.
Hero leader or viral movement frames from ch08.

exampleSpecs.audience: a person whose sleepwalking has stopped feeling mysterious after two documented hallway incidents
exampleSpecs.stakes: a stranger, staff member, or the traveler could be hurt if the same nighttime loop is treated as unknowable again
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: At check-in, he looks at the folded sleep-clinic note, feels the old embarrassment, then asks for a door-alarm wedge and ground-floor room because the hallway loop is now foreseeable enough to contain before sleep.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A folded sleep-clinic note rests beside a hotel key packet.
mustAvoid: excusing harm because the action is automatic

exampleSpecs.domain: ride-share driver after repeated lane-drift warnings on overnight shifts
exampleSpecs.audience: a driver who has treated the warning chime as annoying instead of evidence of a predictable loop
exampleSpecs.stakes: a passenger and other drivers share the risk once the drowsy-shift pattern is visible
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: After printing the lane-alert log, she circles the same 3 a.m. drift pattern and blocks overnight rides in the app before the next weekend, accepting that the known cue now creates a duty to avoid it.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A lane-alert log curls from a dashboard printer.

exampleSpecs.domain: community rocketry club launch-controller arming sequence
exampleSpecs.audience: a volunteer safety officer after a near misfire shows one member always skips the verbal arming call
exampleSpecs.stakes: spectators and students stand behind a rope line that depends on a sequence everyone can verify
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: The safety officer can call the member careless, but instead holds up the brass arming key, names the skipped call as a foreseeable loop, and installs a two-voice callout before the key can turn.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A brass arming key hangs from a launch-controller switch.

exampleSpecs.domain: accounts-payable wire approval after a familiar-sender phishing attempt
exampleSpecs.audience: a finance controller whose team learned that month-end pressure makes one shortcut predictable
exampleSpecs.stakes: a single automatic approval could move six figures before anyone notices the false vendor domain
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: The controller predicts the next fake invoice will arrive near close, then makes the analyst hover over the vendor domain and place the orange hold flag before approval, turning awareness into a redesigned gate.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: An orange hold flag sits beside a month-end invoice queue.

exampleSpecs.domain: darkroom photographer disposing of chemical fixer after late print sessions
exampleSpecs.audience: a studio owner who now knows fatigue makes the sink-pour routine likely after midnight
exampleSpecs.stakes: hazardous chemical disposal is not excused once the cue, shortcut, and harm are predictable
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Before the redesign, the black fixer jug sits beside the sink after late sessions; after the complaint, the owner chains the jug to a silver recovery can and locks the sink cover before printing starts.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A black fixer jug sits beside a stainless sink in the darkroom.

exampleSpecs.domain: glassblowing studio torch valve left open during applause breaks
exampleSpecs.audience: a studio director whose best demonstrator keeps missing one shutoff step when the crowd claps
exampleSpecs.stakes: students and visitors are exposed to a known gas risk if the studio treats applause as a harmless distraction
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: The director taps the cold torch valve tag and says the applause cue is now known, then moves the demonstration line behind a shutoff-and-point routine that must happen before anyone bows.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A cold torch valve tag dangles beside a cooling glass gather.

skillTargets: distinguish habit explanation from habit excuse once awareness and foreseeability are present
identify when a risky loop creates a duty to contain, redesign, or avoid trigger conditions
choose responses that change conditions before the next exposure instead of relying on remorse or vague awareness
evaluate whether accountability is being handled as simple blame, broad philosophy, or practical redesign

tryThisNowSpec: Name one loop that could hurt someone if repeated. Write the cue, the likely harm, and the containment you would put in place before the next cue appears.
